That's quite a lofty goal 😄  Not possible without a complete re-architecture of starship.

A global timeout actually seems like a pretty reasonable idea.

As an aside, right now we do `Repository::discover`, even if all of the git features are disabled - which we should address. I guess this is related to #283

Unfortunately, asynchronous rendering will not be possible for quite a while (possibly not even until version 2.0!) since it requires very deep integration with the shell.

However, it should be entirely possible to do a timeout for the module. I've opened an issue specifically for the timeout on #312.
For prior-art, the popular "pure" prompt for ZSH does this asynchronously: https://github.com/sindresorhus/pure

this, 1000 times this. I've given up on every prompt generator because of this (and pure is npm so I don't want it). 
Even though I have an SSD, as soon as I enter a kernel tree or some big repository, I have to  wait seconds. Surely there must be a faster dirty way to accomplish this with starship (let me hope :D) ?

Is it possible to ignore a certain folder (and subfolders) for now? I couldn't find some doc about it.

I had to disable starship entirely because of one large repo I'm working on and I can't wait ~2s everytime I need to run a command :smile:

> For prior-art, the popular "pure" prompt for ZSH does this asynchronously: https://github.com/sindresorhus/pure

The state of the art in Git prompts is https://github.com/romkatv/gitstatus. It's at least 10x faster than any other Git prompt. 40 times faster than libgit2 that Starship uses. It can be used as a standalone prompt (bash/zsh) or as a building block for a theme. For example, [Powerlevel10k](https://github.com/romkatv/powerlevel10k/) -- arguably the fastest and most flexible zsh theme -- is using gitstatus. It takes Starship 1.8 seconds to render prompt in a chromium Git repo. Powerlevel10k does the same in 45 milliseconds.

I'd also ask if it's possible to have the git bits of the prompt ignore submodules. One of the repos I use has about 12 submodules in its main directory. libgit2 be *slow* inside there and each prompt draw by `starship` is about 5 seconds at a minimum.

@mathomp4 Care to try https://github.com/romkatv/gitstatus just to compare latency?

```zsh
git clone https://github.com/romkatv/gitstatus.git ~/gitstatus
```

Bash:

1. `bash --norc`
2. `source ~/gitstatus/gitstatus.prompt.sh`

Zsh:

1. `zsh -f`
2. `source ~/gitstatus/gitstatus.prompt.zsh`

@romkatv Definitely faster! Pretty much instant. Seems to handle the submodules in a happier manner.

Of course, not as fancy as `starship`. Maybe it's time to ask my sysadmins at upgrading my local box to have a recent zsh (whatever RPM it is is quite old).

> Of course, not as fancy as `starship`.

@mathomp4 What you've tried is essentially an example of how to integrate gitstatusd with your prompt. If you are looking for a full-fledged theme that integrates with gitstatusd, try [powerlevel10k](https://github.com/romkatv/powerlevel10k/). It's more feature-rich than starship, has flexible styling (from minimalist to ridiculous), easier to configure, has faster prompt and can even make your zsh start *faster* than if you didn't use any theme at all (see [instant prompt](https://github.com/romkatv/powerlevel10k/blob/master/README.md#what-is-instant-prompt)). The caveat is that it requires zsh >= 5.1 to function and zsh >= 5.4 to be fast, while starship works pretty much everywhere.

And that's one reason I've been using starship. I work on clusters where the bash is still in v3 land and the zsh isn't even an allowed login shell. Thankfully a MUSL build of starship seems to work there.
@romkatv I've been toying with the idea of using https://github.com/romkatv/gitstatus via FFI in Starship. You've really done great work around it, and we'd love to speed up our git status calls. 😄

> And that's one reason I've been using starship. I work on clusters where the bash is still in v3 land and the zsh isn't even an allowed login shell. Thankfully a MUSL build of starship seems to work there.

Interesting. If you can install starship, cannot you also install zsh? I understand that you won't be able to set zsh as your login shell, but you also cannot set starthsip as shell, can you? I suppose you are enabling starship via `~/.bashrc`. You could similarly "enable" zsh with `exec zsh`.

Basically, if you can to install *some* external userland software, then you can install *any* external userland software. The only real constraint is the kernel version.

> @romkatv I've been toying with the idea of using https://github.com/romkatv/gitstatus via FFI in Starship.

Could you share any details? https://github.com/romkatv/gitstatus is a binary, not a library. You could yank pieces out of it and turn them into a library, but this would come with 10x slowdown. It would still be 4x faster than libgit2 and on par with regular `git status`, but at that point you might as well just call `git status --porcelain=2 -b` and parse its output.

> https://github.com/romkatv/gitstatus is a binary, not a library. You could yank pieces out of it and turn them into a library, but this would come with 10x slowdown. It would still be 4x faster than libgit2 and on par with regular git status, but at that point you might as well just call git status --porcelain=2 -b and parse its output.

Ah interesting. Thanks for the heads up! Yeah, I was planning on using parts of it as a library, but if there are performance repurcussions, it could certainly be used as a binary. I'll be doing some experimentation. 👍

> Ah interesting. Thanks for the heads up! Yeah, I was planning on using parts of it as a library, but if there are performance repurcussions, it could certainly be used as a binary. I'll be doing some experimentation.

@romkatv I couple of questions:

> Keep in mind that the distribution story for gistatusd is quite awful. It shouldn't affect your experiments but releasing integration with gitstatusd to all starship users is a different matter.

Out of curiosity, why is gitstatusd an awful distribution problem?

On the other hand:
> You could yank pieces out of it and turn them into a library, but this would come with 10x slowdown.

Why will there be such slowdown? Because of FFI?

> @romkatv I couple of questions:
> 
> > Keep in mind that the distribution story for gistatusd is quite awful. It shouldn't affect your experiments but releasing integration with gitstatusd to all starship users is a different matter.
> 
> Out of curiosity, why is gitstatusd an awful distribution problem?

If you are asking how gitstatusd binaries are distributed, the answer is that I commit them into the same repo where source code is located: https://github.com/romkatv/gitstatus/tree/master/bin.

If your questions is about *why* I'm doing this, then I suppose I don't know any better.

> Why will there be such slowdown? Because of FFI?

Because gitstatusd maintains expensive state. If you spawn gitstatusd, send it one request and shut it down, it's about as fast as plain `git status`. You might as well call `git status` and parse its output. (By the way, this will be a nice performance improvement for starship.)

> You might as well call git status and parse its output. (By the way, this will be a nice performance improvement for starship.)

The reason I opted to use libgit2 instead of `git status` is so that we could provide git context for users that may have misconfigured git, or not have it installed. That said, I didn't know there would be a considerable performance repercussion to using libgit2. Definitely worth looking into. 👍

> The reason I opted to use libgit2 instead of `git status` is so that we could provide git context for users that may have misconfigured git, or not have it installed.

I think this shouldn't be an issue in practice. I've never encountered anyone with this problem.

> That said, I didn't know there would be a considerable performance repercussion to using libgit2. Definitely worth looking into.

I didn't know either. The first version of gitstatus was similar to starship in terms of architecture -- a binary that is called before every prompt. It also used libgit2. I learned the hard way that libgit2 is slow.

I was going to open a new bug report about this, but I've found that `git status` slows down the Starship prompt quite a bit even in WSL 2, but only in native Windows directories. I'm not sure why this is, but maybe Starship could do something "clever" to detect whether the specified directory is in some kind of "foreign" file system that will cause Git to be slow, and display some sort of iconography to that effect, avoiding `git status` altogether. (This seems like a fairly niche case, because one usually doesn't want to be running a WSL shell when working with native Windows git repos.)

-----------------------------

Because I went to the trouble of gathering information for a bug report before posting this comment, I'll just include that information here:


#### Environment
- Starship version: 0.38.1
- Shell type: Bash
- Shell version: 4.4.20(1)-release, x86_64-pc-linux-gnu
- Terminal emulator: Alacritty, built from a recent master 
- Operating system: Ubuntu Bionic on WSL 2 (Windows 10 v2004, preview slow-ring)

#### Relevant Shell Configuration
I am able to reproduce this using no custom configuration:

```bash
<starship prompt> env -i bash --norc --noprofile
bash-4.4$ time /home/<username>/.cargo/bin/starship prompt
real    0m8.290s
user    0m0.622s
sys    0m1.002s
```
FWIW, when I use wsl, all my git repos are on NTFS. It's not a weird use case.
@romkatv Are you using Windows' native `git` with those repos, or a WSL `git`?
I use git from WSL (and all the rest command line tools from WSL) and store all my data on NTFS.
....actually, if `starship` can detect a native version of Git and use it on NTFS, that would be even slicker.
Isn't WSL git on NTFS slow even outside the context of `starship`?
This doesn't matter neither for starship nor for powerlevel10k. Neither is using `git` command.

> Isn't WSL git on NTFS slow even outside the context of `starship`?

It is. Starship isn't using it though. Starship is using libgit2. It's slower than `git`.
Okay, well, `libgit2` exists on Windows. My point stands: I expect that if a Windows build of `libgit2` can be used, that would substantially speed up fetching the status on NTFS.

> ....actually, if `starship` can detect a native version of Git and use it on NTFS, that would be even slicker.

Native version of git is also slow on NTFS. The problem is in NTFS, not in git.
When I run `time /path/to/git.exe status` and `time git status` on the same directory in NTFS, the `git` version (i.e. the ELF binary in WSL) is about 10x slower.
I don't have a Windows build of `libgit2` handy at the moment, but I'd expect it would also be much faster.

> When I run `time /path/to/git.exe status` and `time git status` on the same directory in NTFS, the `git` version (i.e. the ELF binary in WSL) is about 10x slower.

Fascinating. I don't have wsl2 but with wsl they are roughly equal. Both are abysmally slow. Way too slow to be usable if called synchronously on every prompt.

Hm, if `libgit2` works the same way, where having a Windows native binary for NTFS makes a difference in WSL 2 but not WSL, then any fix should probably wait until WSL 2 is widely available (currently it's only available on preview builds, but I think it will be widely available with the release coming in May).

> having a Windows native binary for NTFS makes a difference in WSL 2 but not WSL

What does this mean?

The data you and I have posted indicates that `git` from WSL2 is slower than `git` from WSL when the repo is on NTFS. Granted, this isn't very scientific (an understatement).

I don't think there can be any difference in performance of native `git.exe` between calling it from WSL or WSL2. It's the same binary that runs on the same kernel. There **can** be a difference between `git` from `WSL` and `WSL2`. Even thought it's the same binary, it runs on different kernels.

FWIW, gitstatus (and by extension powerlevel10k) is fast on WSL. I haven't measured it on WSL2. No one have complained either.
The windows native exe wouldn't have to go through the VFS layer, not sure about the impact though.

@romkatv I'm not talking about `git` from WSL 1 in any of my posts. I'm comparing Windows `git.exe` to WSL 2 `git`. The Windows-native `git.exe` is presumably always fast when used on repos living in NTFS (I haven't checked how it works when called from WSL 1, but I agree with you that it should be no different from its behavior with WSL 2). The WSL 2 `git` is not fast on these same repos. So I am guessing that a Windows-native `libgit2.dll` would _also_ be faster than the WSL 2 `libgit2.so` when called on NTFS.

If indeed this is the case, then it would be a nice feature for Starship to attempt to use `libgit2.dll` when the current directory is NTFS. (I'm not sure how this would work from within the WSL process, though, since presumably linking against DLLs is not supported.)

> The Windows-native `git.exe` is presumably always fast when used on repos living in NTFS

It's slow.

> So I am guessing that a Windows-native `libgit2.dll` would _also_ be faster than the WSL 2 `libgit2.so` when called on NTFS.

`libgit2.dll` is even slower than `git.exe`.

Your posts indicate that `git` from WSL2 is slower than `git.exe` by a factor of 10. This is bad news but it's mostly of theoretical concern. `git.exe` is already too slow to be used in prompts.

So, Starship is currently using `libgit2.so`, which is slower than `libgit2.dll`, which is slower than `git.exe`, which is "too slow to be used in prompts". If indeed `libgit2.dll` wouldn't be fast enough for prompts (which I'm not quite convinced of, since on my machine `git.exe` seems quite fast), then that brings me back to the suggestion from my original comment, which was for Starship to skip fetching Git status entirely when on an NTFS filesystem in a WSL shell.
Poor NTFS performance in WSL1 and WSL2 is [well documented](https://github.com/microsoft/WSL/issues/4197) - I don't see this as a high priority for us to solve.

I realize that this is a tall order, but I wanted to throw it out there. If I had infinite money, I would throw money at someone to use [gitoxide](https://github.com/Byron/gitoxide) to write a Rust-powered [`gitstatusd`](https://github.com/romkatv/gitstatus) that could also be used as a library.

Then `starship` could then utilize this library:
* Starship could remain a single deployable binary - it could respawn itself in daemon mode to do the necessary caching tasks
* Starship could use the user's configuration to alter how it uses this supposed library to track the repo (some of us don't need extensive info and just want dirty status, so the overall memory usage could be reduced)
* Presumably extensive performance tricks could be used. Instead of having to LD_PRELOAD to modify filesystem behavior, gitoxide could be utilized directly, or potentially extended to include further optimizations.

(Beyond this being a bunch of new code to author, I'm not sure `gitoxide` is feature-complete enough to be able to implement `gitstatusd` in it. But I have day-dreamed about it a few times and wanted to throw it out there.)

@colemickens That would be cool, but I don't think it would actually fix all the issues described here. Specifically, I suspect that any Linux implementation of Git (even one in Rust) would always be slow when trying to read data from a Windows git repository from within a WSL process. (I still suspect that the best way to handle this case is to simply not attempt any git operations across network filesystem boundaries.)

I was curious to see what it would take to integrate the bash/zsh bindings of [gitstatus](https://github.com/romkatv/gitstatus) into starship and at first glance, it seems very straight forward to replace the current git parsing logic with something which get these infos from gitstatusd. The tricky part seems to be to get access to the running gitstatusd daemon: if I understand the design correctly, every shell instance would have it's own gitstatus daemon running and the interaction happens via some FIFO FDs which are available via two unexported env variables. One would need ask the user (or do it in the `starship init` part) to export the right env variables so these are available in starship. As far as I understand, these env variables are different between bash and zsh (zsh contains the "name" in the env variable, bash does not?). So the story would be something like this (zsh version with "NAME" as name): ```zsh source ~/gitstatus/gitstatus.plugin.zsh gitstatus_stop 'NAME' && gitstatus_start -s -1 -u -1 -c -1 -d -1 'NAME' export _GITSTATUS_REQ_FD_NAME export _GITSTATUS_RESP_FD_NAME # starship init here... ``` An alternative would be to demonize gitstatusd in the `starship init` script, but this seems to be a lot of additional work but would probably help on non-bash/zsh shells :-/ The git integration in starship would then need to add a config (with sensible defaults) which specifies how the env variables are named which contain the REQ and RESP end of the fifo. The [actual parsing](https://github.com/romkatv/gitstatus/blob/master/gitstatus.plugin.sh#L392-L431) (see below for all the available fields) seems to be straight forward and would then be pushed into the [current data structure](https://github.com/starship/starship/blob/master/src/modules/git_status.rs#L262-L272).(1) (1) Ok, there is the point that this call actually exposes stuff like the branch name, commit id and more which is reusable by the other git_* modules: seems there is nothing missing, so this is actually useable as a complete replacement for all of the modules! So it might make sense to actually push that computation into the shared context and use it from all? That would replace at least two git calls and probably a few more libgit2 operations...
Available fields

``` 1. Request id. The same as the first field in the request. 2. 0 if the directory isn't a git repo, 1 otherwise. If 0, all the following fields are missing. 3. Absolute path to the git repository workdir. 4. Commit hash that HEAD is pointing to. 40 hex digits. 5. Local branch name or empty if not on a branch. 6. Upstream branch name. Can be empty. 7. The remote name, e.g. "upstream" or "origin". 8. Remote URL. Can be empty. 9. Repository state, A.K.A. action. Can be empty. 10. The number of files in the index. 11. The number of staged changes. 12. The number of unstaged changes. 13. The number of conflicted changes. 14. The number of untracked files. 15. Number of commits the current branch is ahead of upstream. 16. Number of commits the current branch is behind upstream. 17. The number of stashes. 18. The last tag (in lexicographical order) that points to the same commit as HEAD. 19. The number of unstaged deleted files. 20. The number of staged new files. 21. The number of staged deleted files. 22. The push remote name, e.g. "upstream" or "origin". 23. Push remote URL. Can be empty. 24. Number of commits the current branch is ahead of push remote. 25. Number of commits the current branch is behind push remote. 26. Number of files in the index with skip-worktree bit set. 27. Number of files in the index with assume-unchanged bit set. 28. Encoding of the HEAD's commit message. Empty value means UTF-8. 29. The first paragraph of the HEAD's commit message as one line. ```
